summaries.example: Imagine saying, “A triangle has three sides,” even when no triangle is in the room. Simon would say this can still be true because the words and ideas have meaning, and being three-sided belongs to what a triangle is. The statement does not need a particular triangle sitting nearby.
summaries.summary: Simon of Faversham was an English scholar who lived around 1260–1306. He taught at universities in Oxford and Paris and became known for explaining Aristotle’s works. His writings were mostly commentaries, which means detailed discussions of earlier books. Simon wrote about logic, the mind, nature, and metaphysics—the study of reality and what things are. In logic, he said that reasoning helps us learn new things from things we already know. He also studied how words get their meaning. He believed that words such as “human” point to an essence, or what something is, rather than only pointing to a picture or idea in someone’s mind. He offered an interesting view of truth: a statement about an essence can be true even if no real example exists at that moment. He also explained universals as ways the mind understands a nature that can belong to many individuals. His work is important because it shows how medieval thinkers developed ideas about language, reasoning, knowledge, and reality.
key_ideas: Simon of Faversham was a thirteenth-century scholar who wrote many commentaries on Aristotle.
He thought logic was a tool for learning, not just a subject to study by itself.
He argued that ordinary words such as “human” can signify things or essences, not only ideas in the mind.
He explored how a statement can be true even when the thing it talks about does not currently exist.
He also wrote about the mind, dreams, universals, essence, and existence.
summaries.why_it_matters: Simon’s work shows that people long ago asked questions that still matter: How do words mean things? How can we tell whether an argument is good? Can a sentence be true when its subject is not present? His writings also show that philosophy grows through discussion with earlier thinkers. Studying him helps us see how ideas about language, science, the mind, and reality changed during the Middle Ages.

important_terms.definition: A careful way of thinking that helps us move from things we already know to things we do not yet know.
The basic nature of what a thing is, such as what makes a human a human.
The meaning or thing connected to a word or sign.
A statement or belief that agrees with how things are.
A general idea that can apply to more than one individual, such as “human.”

questions_to_think_about: Can a sentence be meaningful even if nothing nearby matches it?
What is the difference between a thing and an idea of that thing?
Why might people need rules for reasoning?
Can one general idea describe many different individual things?

summaries.example: Consider the statement “The human is an animal.” Simon argues that this essential predication can remain true even if no individual human exists. The subject and predicate still express and signify the relevant essences, and being an animal belongs to the definition of being human. This differs from “The human is running,” whose truth would require an actual running human because running is an accidental, real-world property.
summaries.summary: Simon of Faversham was a British scholar of the late thirteenth century, educated and active at Oxford and Paris, whose surviving corpus consists largely of commentaries on Aristotle and related logical texts. The entry emphasizes both the uneven state of some of his discussions and the originality of others. In logic, Simon identifies the subject matter with methods of acquiring knowledge: definition, division, and especially syllogistic inference. He presents five kinds of syllogism, distinguished by the status of their premises and conclusions, and includes rhetoric and poetics within this broad logical division. In the debate over signification, he rejects the position that words of first imposition immediately signify concepts. Such words instead signify essences, though signification depends on a speaker’s expression and a listener’s conceptual understanding. His treatment of truth extends adequation beyond composite judgments to the intellect’s apprehension of essences. In essential predication, a statement can be true without an external instance, provided the relevant essences are conceptualized and signified. Simon also argues that universality is a mental mode of considering an essence rather than an independently existing universal. His wider views concern Aristotelian psychology, abstraction, dreams, individuation, the essence–existence distinction, and the analogy of being.
key_ideas: Simon treats logic as instrumental: it supports the theoretical sciences by organizing ways of moving from known knowledge to unknown knowledge.
He divides reasoning into demonstrative, dialectical, rhetorical, poetic, and sophistical forms according to the kind of premises and conclusion involved.

Against the view that first-imposition words immediately signify concepts, Simon argues that words such as “human” and “stone” signify essences, while still requiring both speaker expression and listener understanding.
His account of truth includes simple apprehension as well as composite judgment, although his most distinctive analysis concerns essential predication and empty reference.
Simon holds that universality belongs to a way the intellect considers an essence; external things are particular, while an essence can be understood as one in many.
His writings also develop Aristotelian positions on the intellect, abstraction, dreams, individuation, essence and existence, and the analogical predication of being.
summaries.why_it_matters: Simon is historically important because his works capture a significant stage in thirteenth-century debates about Aristotelian philosophy. His analyses connect questions that are often studied separately: how language signifies, how judgments become true, how the intellect forms concepts, and how general natures relate to individual things. His positions also reveal philosophy as an ongoing process of adopting, revising, and sometimes combining inherited theories. Since much of his corpus remains understudied or available only in manuscripts, the entry also illustrates how historical knowledge depends on the preservation and interpretation of texts.

important_terms.definition: For Simon, the study of methods for acquiring knowledge, including definition, division, and syllogistic reasoning.
What a thing is, considered through its essential features rather than its accidental conditions.
The semantic relation by which a word expresses or occasions understanding of what it means.
A state in which a belief or intellectual act agrees with its object or with the relevant way things are.
A nature considered by the intellect as capable of belonging to several individuals; it is universal in thought, not as an independently existing universal object.
A structured argument in which premises support a conclusion; Simon divided syllogisms by the certainty or character of their premises.
A mode of being or status dependent on a knowing subject, contrasted with actual existence outside the mind.
The relation between what a thing is and its being in a causally ordered reality; Simon ultimately treats their distinction as notional rather than real.

questions_to_think_about: If a word signifies an essence, what role do the speaker’s intention and the listener’s understanding play?
Should “the human is an animal” be true if no humans exist? What would make it true or false?
Is a universal something existing outside the mind, or a way the mind organizes what it understands?
Why might rhetoric and poetry be treated as types of syllogistic reasoning?
Does distinguishing essence from existence require two really separate things, or can the distinction be conceptual?

summaries.example: Suppose someone says, “Dragons are reptiles.” You might ask whether this can be true if dragons do not exist. Simon’s discussion helps separate two cases. A statement about an essential feature can be supported by what the words mean and by the concepts they express. A statement about an accidental feature, such as “the dragon is flying,” would need a real thing that is flying. This is part of Simon’s larger question about how language and truth work.
summaries.summary: Simon of Faversham was a thirteenth-century English scholar who studied and taught at Oxford and Paris and later held academic and church offices. He is mainly known for commentaries on Aristotle’s logical and natural-philosophical works. The source presents him as a thinker whose surviving writings are sometimes incomplete or less developed, but whose strongest discussions show careful analysis. Simon says that logic studies ways of gaining knowledge: defining, dividing, and drawing conclusions through syllogisms. He distinguishes kinds of syllogism by how reliable their starting points are. A demonstration aims at certainty; dialectical reasoning supports an acceptable belief; rhetoric works with suspicion or persuasion; poetry produces an estimation; and sophistical reasoning leads to error. In the debate about meaning, Simon says that words such as “human” signify an essence rather than the concept of that essence. Words for logical notions are different because those notions depend on a knowing mind. Simon also argues that essential claims can be true without existing examples, while claims about real accidents require appropriate things in the world. In his account of universals, an essence is particular in external things but can be understood by the mind as one nature found in many. His other philosophical discussions concern the intellect and abstraction, dreams, individuation, essence and existence, and the way being is predicated of substances and accidents.
key_ideas: Simon of Faversham was a medieval scholar and commentator on Aristotle whose most studied writings concern logic.
He understood logic as a tool for gaining knowledge and discussed several kinds of reasoning, including scientific, everyday, persuasive, poetic, and misleading arguments.
He argued that common words usually signify essences or things rather than concepts alone, although words connected with logical notions signify concepts.
He held that truth can belong to simple understanding as well as to complete judgments, and he gave a special account of statements about essences.
For Simon, universals are not separate objects floating outside the world; they are ways the intellect understands a nature as common to individuals.
His writings also addressed the intellect, dreams, the principle that makes things individuals, and the relationship between essence and existence.
summaries.why_it_matters: Simon helps us understand how medieval philosophers investigated language, reasoning, knowledge, and reality as connected problems. His work is especially useful for seeing why the meaning of a word is not the same question as whether something exists, and why a general concept need not be a separately existing object. His discussions also show that historical philosophers could combine inherited theories in ways that later readers find difficult or internally tense. Reading Simon therefore teaches both philosophical ideas and the importance of examining arguments closely rather than assigning a thinker a simple label.

important_terms.definition: A system for reasoning that helps people move from known information toward new knowledge.
The features that make something the kind of thing it is.
What a word means or points to in communication.
Agreement between a belief or statement and the relevant way things are.
A general nature, such as “human,” that the mind can understand as belonging to many individuals.
An argument with premises that are used to support a conclusion.
A feature that may belong to a thing but is not part of what the thing fundamentally is, such as being white or running.
The fact of being real, present in the world, or present in thought.

questions_to_think_about: What makes an argument scientific rather than merely persuasive?
When you hear the word “tree,” are you understanding a real thing, a mental concept, or both?
Can a general idea be real in the world if every individual thing is particular?
Why might a statement about what something is be treated differently from a statement about what it happens to be doing?
How could two philosophers agree about a topic but disagree about whether a distinction is real or only conceptual?
